terms: Atom

The smallest particle of an element that can exist. Atoms are far too small to see, even with a light microscope: a grain of powder you can see contains a huge number of them. A single atom does not have the properties of a lump of the substance, such as its colour or hardness.
Dalton's atomic model

A simple model of matter put forward by John Dalton in the early 1800s. In Dalton's model: everything is made of tiny atoms that cannot be broken down; all the atoms of one element are identical, and atoms of different elements are different (they have different masses); atoms join in fixed whole-number ratios to make compounds; in a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed. It is a model: it pictures each atom as a tiny solid sphere so that we can explain what we observe.
Chemical reaction

A change in which new substances are made. The atoms in the starting substances (reactants) are rearranged: they separate from the atoms they were joined to and join up in new ways in the products. No atoms are created or destroyed.
Element

A substance made of only one type of atom. An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by a chemical reaction. Some elements are made of atoms that are not joined in molecules (helium, He; iron, Fe); others are made of molecules containing two atoms of that one element (oxygen, O₂; nitrogen, N₂; hydrogen, H₂; chlorine, Cl₂).
Molecule

A particle made of two or more atoms chemically joined (bonded) together. The atoms can be of the same element, as in O₂ and N₂ (elements made of molecules), or of different elements, as in H₂O, CO₂ and CH₄ (compounds made of molecules).
Compound

A substance made of atoms of two or more different elements chemically joined (bonded) together in a fixed ratio, for example water, H₂O (2 hydrogen atoms to 1 oxygen atom), and carbon dioxide, CO₂ (1 carbon atom to 2 oxygen atoms). A compound has properties different from those of its elements, and it can be split up only by a chemical reaction.
Mixture

Two or more substances (elements or compounds) that are together but not chemically joined. The amounts can vary, each substance keeps its own properties, and the substances can be separated without a chemical reaction. Air, salt water, and iron filings stirred into sulfur powder are mixtures.
Chemical symbol

A one- or two-letter code for an element. The first letter is always a capital and a second letter is always lower case: Co is the element cobalt, but CO is carbon (C) and oxygen (O) joined, carbon monoxide. Many symbols come from the English name (H, He, C, N, O, Mg, Al, S, Cl, Ca, Zn); some come from Latin names: Na sodium (natrium), K potassium (kalium), Fe iron (ferrum), Cu copper (cuprum), Ag silver (argentum), Au gold (aurum), Pb lead (plumbum).
Chemical formula

Symbols and numbers that show which elements are in a substance and how many atoms of each there are in one particle (or in what ratio they are joined). Elements made of molecules have formulae (O₂, N₂, H₂, Cl₂) as well as compounds (H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NaCl).
Subscript (small number in a formula)

The small number written after and below a symbol. It counts the atoms of the element just before it; a symbol with no number means one atom. H₂O has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom; C₆H₁₂O₆ has 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 atoms. A large number in front means separate particles: 2N is two separate nitrogen atoms, N₂ is one molecule of two joined nitrogen atoms.
Conservation of mass

In a change of state, in dissolving and in a chemical reaction, the total mass stays the same, because the same atoms (particles) are there before and after. Total mass before = total mass after; for a reaction, mass of reactants = mass of products.
Reactants and products
Reactants are the substances you start with in a chemical reaction; products are the new substances made. In a word equation an arrow separates them: iron + sulfur → iron sulfide.
Closed (sealed) container
A container that nothing can get into or out of, such as a sealed flask or bag. The mass of a sealed container and its contents stays the same whatever change happens inside.
Open container

A container open to the air. If a gas is made and escapes, the measured mass goes down; if a gas from the air, such as oxygen, joins on, the measured mass goes up. Total mass is still conserved: the balance simply does not weigh gas that has left or that was in the air before.
Dissolving

When a solid spreads out as separate particles between the particles of a liquid, making a solution. The solid is still there (evaporating the water gives it back), so the mass of the solution = mass of liquid + mass of solid.
Change of state

Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and subliming (a solid turning straight into a gas). The particles are arranged differently and move differently, but no particles are made or lost, so the mass stays the same.

terms: Particle model

A scientific model in which all matter is made of huge numbers of tiny particles that are always moving. The particles are far too small to see, even with a microscope. Solid, liquid and gas forms of one substance contain the same particles: what is different is how the particles are arranged, how close together they are and how they move. The particles themselves do not change size, melt or boil, and the spaces between them are empty.
Solid

A state of matter in which the particles are close together (touching), held in fixed places, usually in a regular pattern, and vibrate on the spot. Because the particles cannot move past each other, a solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume, cannot flow, and can hardly be squashed.
Liquid

A state of matter in which the particles are close together (touching) but arranged randomly, with no pattern. They move around and slide past each other. So a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container, can flow (be poured), and can hardly be squashed.
Gas

A state of matter in which the particles are far apart, with empty space between them, arranged randomly and moving quickly in all directions. So a gas has no fixed shape or volume, spreads out to fill any container it is in, and can be squashed easily.
Compress (squash)

To push a substance into a smaller volume. A gas can be compressed easily because there is a lot of empty space between its particles. Solids and liquids can hardly be compressed at all, because their particles are already touching.
Gas pressure

The push of a gas on the walls of its container. It is caused by the gas particles hitting the walls: each hit gives a tiny push, and huge numbers of hits every second add up to the pressure. A gas that is just sitting still in a container still has a pressure, because its particles are always moving.
Heating a gas in a sealed container
If a gas is heated in a container that cannot get bigger, its particles move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises. The particles do not get bigger.
Squashing a gas

If a gas is pushed into a smaller volume and kept at the same temperature, its particles are closer together and hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises. The particles themselves are not squashed.
Change of state

A change between solid, liquid and gas, such as melting or boiling. It is a physical change: no new substance is made, the particles stay the same and the mass stays the same. Only the arrangement, closeness and movement of the particles change. Energy is transferred to a substance to melt or boil it, and from it when it freezes or condenses.
Melting

The change from solid to liquid. Energy is transferred to the solid; its particles vibrate faster until they break out of their fixed places and can move around each other. A pure substance melts at a fixed temperature, its melting point (ice melts at 0 °C).
Freezing

The change from liquid to solid. Energy is transferred from the liquid to its colder surroundings; its particles settle into fixed places, where they can only vibrate. A pure substance freezes at the same temperature as it melts.
Boiling

The change from liquid to gas that happens all through the liquid, at one temperature: the boiling point (100 °C for pure water at normal air pressure). Energy is transferred to the liquid, and bubbles of the substance's own gas form inside the liquid and rise.
Evaporating

The change from liquid to gas that happens only at the surface of the liquid, and can happen at temperatures well below the boiling point. The fastest-moving particles at the surface escape into the air. Puddles and wet washing dry by evaporation.
Condensing

The change from gas to liquid. Energy is transferred from the gas, for example when it touches a cold surface; its particles come close together as a liquid. Water vapour in the air condenses into drops on a cold window or a cold can.
Sublimation

The change from solid straight to gas, with no liquid in between. Particles break free from the solid and move apart as a gas. For example, solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) sublimes at room temperature.
Water vapour

Water in the gas state. Like most gases it is invisible. The white cloud above a kettle and the mist on a cold morning are not water vapour: they are tiny drops of liquid water that have condensed from it.
Pure substance

In science, a pure substance is a single substance with nothing else mixed in: one element (such as copper) or one compound (such as water). In everyday life 'pure' often means natural, clean or with nothing added; that is not the scientific meaning.
Impure substance
A material that has more than one substance in it. Any mixture is impure, even one that looks clear or is natural, such as sea water, spring water or air.
Mixture

Two or more substances that are together but not chemically joined. The amount of each can vary, each keeps its own properties, and they can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography.
Dissolving

When a solid (or other substance) spreads out as separate particles among the particles of a liquid to make a solution. The dissolved substance is still there, so its mass is still there. Dissolving is not melting: no heating of the solid to its melting point is needed.
Solute
The substance that dissolves, for example the salt in salty water or the sugar in sweet tea.
Solvent
The liquid that the solute dissolves in, for example the water in salty water.
Solution
The mixture made when a solute dissolves in a solvent. A solution is see-through (it may be coloured), and the solute does not settle out when it is left to stand.
Soluble and insoluble

A soluble substance dissolves in a given solvent (salt and sugar in water). An insoluble substance does not (sand and chalk in water): it stays as bits that settle or float, and it can be filtered out.
Saturated solution
A solution in which no more solute will dissolve at that temperature. Extra solid added to it stays undissolved, however long you stir.
Solubility

How much of a solute will dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature, for example the mass that dissolves in 100 g of water. For most solids it is higher in hotter water. If a saturated solution is cooled, the solid that can no longer stay dissolved comes out as crystals.
Diffusion

The spreading out and mixing of particles of gases or liquids caused by the random movement of the particles themselves; nothing has to push or stir them. There is an overall (net) movement from where there are more of the particles (higher concentration) to where there are fewer (lower concentration).
Concentration
How much of a substance there is in a given volume. In diffusion, particles spread from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated until they are evenly mixed.
Random movement of particles

In the particle model, particles of liquids and gases move about all the time in all directions, bumping into each other. They do not stop when a mixture is even, and they move faster at a higher temperature, so diffusion is faster when it is hotter.
Filtration

A method that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper: the liquid, with anything dissolved in it, passes through the tiny holes; the bits of insoluble solid are too big and are trapped. The solid left on the paper is the residue; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
Evaporation (to separate a dissolved solid)

A method that gets a dissolved solid back from a solution. The solution is heated in an evaporating dish: the solvent turns to vapour and escapes into the air, and the solid is left behind as crystals. The solvent is lost, not collected.
Distillation

A method that gets the solvent back from a solution. The solution is boiled: the solvent particles escape as a gas, are cooled in a condenser and turn back into liquid (the distillate), which is collected. The dissolved solid has a much higher boiling point, so it stays in the flask.
Paper chromatography

A method that separates a mixture of dissolved substances, such as the dyes in an ink. A spot of the mixture is put on a pencil start line above the solvent; the solvent soaks up the paper and carries each dye a different distance, depending on how well it dissolves in the solvent and how strongly it sticks to the paper. The result is a chromatogram.
Melting point and boiling point
The temperature at which a solid melts, and the temperature at which a liquid boils. Each pure substance has its own values: pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal air pressure.
Sharp point and range

A pure substance melts (or boils) at one fixed temperature: the temperature stays the same until it has all melted (or boiled). A mixture melts or boils over a range of temperatures, usually different from those of the pure substance; salty water, for example, boils above 100 °C.
Testing purity

To test whether a sample is pure, measure its melting point or boiling point and compare it with the value for the pure substance, or run a chromatogram: a pure substance gives a sharp point matching the known value, and only one spot in chromatography.
Chemical reaction

A change in which new substances are made. The atoms in the starting substances separate from the atoms they were joined to and join up in new ways. No atom is made, destroyed or changed into a different kind of atom.
Reactants and products
Reactants are the substances you start with in a reaction. Products are the new substances made. Products have different properties from the reactants.
Physical change

A change in which no new substance is made, such as melting, boiling, condensing or dissolving. The particles stay the same; only their arrangement or spacing changes, and the change can usually be reversed.
Signs of a chemical reaction

Clues that a new substance may have formed: a gas given off that was not there before, a new solid appearing, a lasting colour change, or the mixture getting hot or cold. They are clues, not proof: mixing paints changes colour and boiling makes bubbles without any new substance.
Word equation

A way of showing a reaction with the names of the substances: reactants on the left, products on the right, joined by an arrow that means 'reacts to make'. Example: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.
Symbol equation
A way of showing a reaction with chemical formulae, for example 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. It shows which atoms are in each substance and how many of each substance react.
Balancing number

A big number written in front of a formula in a symbol equation. It shows how many of that molecule (or unit) take part, and it multiplies every atom in the formula: 2H₂O means two water molecules, with 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen atoms. A formula with no big number in front means one.
Balanced equation

A symbol equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, because atoms are not made or destroyed in a reaction. You balance an equation by changing the big numbers in front of formulae, never the small numbers inside a formula.
Combustion

Burning: a reaction of a substance with oxygen that transfers energy to the surroundings as heat and light. A fuel made of carbon and hydrogen (such as methane) burning in plenty of air makes carbon dioxide and water. A metal burns to make its oxide, for example magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. When oxygen is limited, some carbon monoxide and soot (carbon) form instead.
Fuel
A substance that is burned to transfer energy, such as methane, butane, petrol or wax. Its atoms are not destroyed when it burns: they end up in the gases made.
Thermal decomposition
A reaction in which heating breaks one compound down into two or more simpler substances. Many metal carbonates do this: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide.
Oxidation
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. Burning is fast oxidation; rusting is slow oxidation of iron, which needs both oxygen and water. Heating copper in air oxidises it to black copper oxide.
Displacement reaction

A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in its compound, pushing it out. Example: iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper. A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one.
Acid
A substance that is neutralised by an alkali. Acids have a pH below 7 and turn blue litmus red. Examples: hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, nitric acid, citric acid (in lemons) and vinegar.
Alkali

A base that dissolves in water. An alkali neutralises an acid. Alkali solutions have a pH above 7 and turn red litmus blue. Example: sodium hydroxide solution. Alkalis can damage skin and eyes just as acids can.
Neutralisation

The reaction between an acid and an alkali (or another base). It makes new substances, a salt and water, and moves the pH towards 7. It is a reaction, so some acid is neutralised as soon as any alkali is added.
pH scale

A scale, usually 0 to 14, that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is. Below 7 is acidic (the lower the number, the more acidic), 7 is neutral, and above 7 is alkaline (the higher the number, the more alkaline).
Neutral
Neither acidic nor alkaline: pH 7. Pure water is neutral.
Indicator
A substance that changes colour depending on how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
Universal indicator

An indicator with a range of colours that shows the pH number: red or orange for acids (low pH), green for neutral (pH 7), blue or purple for alkalis (high pH). You find the pH by matching the colour to a chart.
Litmus

An indicator that only shows acid or alkali: litmus is red in acids and blue in alkalis. Blue litmus paper turns red in an acid; red litmus paper turns blue in an alkali. Neither changes in a neutral solution.
Salt

A compound made, along with hydrogen or water, when an acid reacts with a metal or a base such as an alkali. Its name has two parts: the first usually comes from the metal, the second from the acid. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates and nitric acid makes nitrates. Sodium chloride (table salt) is just one salt.
Acid + metal reaction
Many metals, such as magnesium and zinc, react with acids: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Bubbles of hydrogen fizz off and the metal is used up as its atoms go into the salt, which stays dissolved.
Test for hydrogen
Hold a lit splint at the mouth of a test tube of the gas. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.
Acid + alkali reaction

acid + alkali → salt + water. For example, hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water. If exactly enough sodium hydroxide is added to hydrochloric acid, the solution ends at pH 7; evaporating the water then leaves the salt.
Catalyst

A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up. The same mass of catalyst is left at the end, so it can be used again. The reaction makes the same products, in the same amount, just faster. Enzymes are catalysts in living things.
Change of state

A change from one state (solid, liquid or gas) to another: melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating and condensing. It is a physical change: no new substance is made, so ice, liquid water and steam are all water. Energy is still transferred during a change of state.
Changes of state that take in energy

Melting, boiling and evaporating take in energy, for example from a flame, a hot plate, the air or your skin. Evaporation takes in energy even when nothing hot is nearby: the energy comes from the liquid left behind and from its surroundings, which is why evaporating sweat cools you.
Changes of state that give out energy

When a substance condenses (gas to liquid) or freezes (liquid to solid), energy is transferred from the substance to its surroundings. This happens even when the freezing point is very high: liquid iron freezes at 1538 °C and gives out energy as it does.
Melting point and boiling point

The temperature at which a pure substance melts (it freezes at the same temperature) and the temperature at which it boils. Each substance has its own values: pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal air pressure; pure iron melts at 1538 °C.
Temperature during a change of state

While a pure substance is melting or boiling, its temperature stays the same even though heating continues. The energy transferred to it changes its state instead of raising its temperature. When the change is complete, the temperature starts to change again.
Temperature and energy

Temperature tells you how hot something is; it is measured in degrees Celsius (°C) with a thermometer. Energy is measured in joules (J). Heating transfers energy, but a substance can take in energy without getting hotter, as in melting and boiling. Cold is not a thing that moves: an object cools when energy is transferred out of it.
Surroundings

Everything around the reacting chemicals that energy can be transferred to or from: the water or solution they are in, the container, the thermometer and the air. A thermometer in the reaction mixture shows what is happening to the temperature of the surroundings.
Exothermic reaction

A chemical reaction that transfers energy to its surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. Examples: combustion (burning fuels), an acid neutralising an alkali, respiration in cells, and the iron powder in a hand warmer reacting with oxygen.
Endothermic reaction

A chemical reaction that takes in energy from its surroundings. Either the temperature of the surroundings falls (citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate), or energy has to be supplied all the time by heating or by light (thermal decomposition, photosynthesis), and the reaction stops when the supply stops.
Thermal decomposition

A reaction in which a substance breaks down into simpler substances when it is heated, for example calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. It is endothermic: the substance takes in energy from the heating as it breaks down, so it keeps breaking down only while it is heated.
Combustion (burning)

The reaction of a fuel with oxygen. Most fuels need a flame or spark to start burning, but once burning has started it gives out far more energy than the spark supplied and keeps going by itself, so it is exothermic.
Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. In an exothermic reaction energy is transferred from the reacting chemicals to the surroundings; in an endothermic reaction it is transferred from the surroundings to the chemicals. The total amount of energy stays the same.
Physical change and chemical reaction

In a chemical reaction new substances are made. In a physical change, such as melting, freezing or dissolving, no new substance is made. 'Exothermic reaction' and 'endothermic reaction' describe chemical reactions; changes of state also take in or give out energy, but they are not reactions.
Element

A substance made of only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by a chemical reaction. About 118 elements are known, and each has a symbol of one or two letters, the first a capital: O (oxygen), Na (sodium), Fe (iron).
Physical property

A property you can observe or measure without making a new substance: for example the state at room temperature, colour, shine, melting point, boiling point and whether the element conducts electricity.
Chemical property

A property that shows how a substance reacts to make new substances. For example, magnesium burns in air to make magnesium oxide, and sodium reacts with water to make hydrogen and an alkaline solution.
Physical change and chemical change

In a physical change, such as melting, boiling or dissolving, no new substance is made and the change can usually be reversed. In a chemical change (a reaction), such as burning, new substances are made.
Melting point
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. Elements' melting points vary hugely: mercury melts at −39 °C, sodium at 98 °C and iron at 1538 °C.
Boiling point

The temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into a gas. An element is a liquid at room temperature if room temperature is above its melting point and below its boiling point: bromine melts at −7 °C and boils at 59 °C.
Mendeleev's periodic table

In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements then known in order of atomic mass and put elements with similar properties in the same group. He left gaps for elements not yet discovered, predicted their properties, and swapped some pairs, such as tellurium and iodine, so that each element sat with similar elements.
Atomic mass

How heavy an atom of an element is compared with atoms of other elements (once called atomic weight). Hydrogen, the lightest, has an atomic mass of about 1, carbon about 12 and iodine about 127. Mendeleev used atomic masses to order the elements.
Atomic number

The number that gives an element's place in today's periodic table, from hydrogen (1) upwards. Today's table is in order of atomic number. Mendeleev did not know about atomic numbers: they were worked out more than 40 years after his first table.
Gap in Mendeleev's table

A space Mendeleev left for an element he believed existed but had not yet been discovered. From the elements around each gap he predicted the missing element's properties; gallium (found in 1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) later filled gaps and matched his predictions closely.
Periodic table
A table of all the elements in order of atomic number, arranged in rows (periods) so that elements with similar properties line up in columns (groups).
Group
A vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group react in similar ways. In UK school tables the main groups are numbered 1 to 7, then 0 for the noble gases.
Period

A horizontal row of the periodic table. Properties change across a period, from metals on the left to non-metals on the right: Period 3 runs from sodium, a reactive metal, to argon, an unreactive gas.
Staircase line

The zig-zag line in the right-hand part of the periodic table. Metals are to its left and non-metals to its right; most elements are metals. Hydrogen is a non-metal, although tables usually show it away from the other non-metals.
Reactivity
How readily and how vigorously an element reacts. Reactivity can be compared by watching reactions, for example how fast Group 1 metals fizz in water.
Group 1: the alkali metals

Lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium are soft metals that react with water to make hydrogen and an alkaline solution. Reactivity increases going down the group: lithium fizzes gently, potassium bursts into lilac flames.
Group 7: the halogens

Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are coloured, reactive non-metals. Reactivity decreases going down the group, and their states change from gas (fluorine, chlorine) to liquid (bromine) to solid (iodine).
Group 0: the noble gases
Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are colourless gases that hardly react at all. Argon is used inside some light bulbs because the hot filament does not react with it.
Prediction from the periodic table
Because elements in a group react in similar ways and follow a trend, you can predict how an element will react from its place in the table. A test then checks the prediction.
Metal

An element to the left of the staircase line. Metals are typically shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, and solid with high melting points. Exceptions: mercury is a liquid; sodium and potassium are soft and melt below 100 °C; only a few metals, such as iron, nickel and cobalt, are attracted to a magnet.
Non-metal

An element to the right of the staircase line, and hydrogen. Non-metals are typically dull and poor conductors of heat and electricity, and brittle when solid; many are gases. Exceptions: graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity, and graphite and iodine are shiny.
Malleable
Able to be hammered or bent into a new shape without breaking. Most metals are malleable.
Brittle
Breaks or shatters when hit or bent. Solid non-metals such as sulfur are brittle.
Conductor and insulator
A conductor lets electricity (or heat) pass through it easily; an insulator does not. Metals are good conductors; most non-metals are insulators, but graphite conducts electricity.
Oxide
A compound of an element with oxygen, often made by burning the element in air or oxygen: magnesium oxide, sulfur dioxide, carbon dioxide.
pH scale
A scale from 0 to 14 that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline. Universal indicator changes colour to show the pH.
Base
A substance that neutralises an acid. The oxides of metals such as sodium, calcium, magnesium and copper are bases.
Alkali

A base that dissolves in water, making an alkaline solution (pH above 7). Sodium oxide and calcium oxide dissolve to make alkaline solutions; copper oxide is a base that does not dissolve, so it is not an alkali.
Metal oxides and non-metal oxides

Oxides of metals such as sodium, calcium and copper are bases; those that dissolve make alkaline solutions. Oxides of non-metals that dissolve, such as sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide, make acidic solutions. A few non-metal oxides, such as water and carbon monoxide, are neutral.
Reactivity series

A list of metals in order of how readily they react, with the most reactive at the top. The KS3 order is: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, lead, copper, silver, gold. Carbon is a non-metal, but it is placed in the list because its position shows which metals it can extract.
Reactive and unreactive metals

A reactive metal reacts quickly and strongly with water, dilute acids and oxygen (potassium and sodium react fast even with cold water). An unreactive metal reacts slowly or not at all (copper, silver and gold do not react with water, dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulfuric acid). The faster the bubbling or the more vigorous the reaction, the higher the metal is in the series.
How the order is found

Metals are put in order by comparing how they react under the same conditions: same-sized pieces in cold water, or in the same dilute acid. More bubbles, more heat or a faster reaction means a more reactive metal.
Ore

A rock that contains enough of a metal compound (often the metal oxide) to make it worth extracting the metal. Only a few very unreactive metals, such as gold, are found in the ground as the pure metal.
Metal oxide

A compound of a metal and oxygen, such as iron oxide or copper oxide. The metal and oxygen are chemically joined, not just mixed, so a chemical reaction is needed to separate them: heating iron oxide or copper oxide on its own does not give the metal.
Extraction
Getting a metal out of its compound in an ore. For a metal oxide, the oxygen must be removed by a chemical reaction.
Reduction
At KS3: loss of oxygen. When carbon takes the oxygen from a metal oxide, the metal oxide is reduced and the metal is left. In science 'reduced' does not mean made smaller.
Oxidation
At KS3: gain of oxygen. When carbon takes oxygen from a metal oxide, the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide. Reduction and oxidation happen together.
Extracting metals with carbon

A metal below carbon in the reactivity series (zinc, iron, lead, copper) can be extracted by heating its oxide strongly with carbon. Carbon is more reactive than the metal, so it takes the oxygen: metal oxide + carbon → metal + carbon dioxide (for example, iron oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide). Metals above carbon (potassium to aluminium) cannot be extracted this way.
Electrolysis
A method that uses electricity to split a compound. It is used to extract metals that are above carbon in the reactivity series, such as aluminium. How it works is GCSE content.
Ceramic

A hard material made by heating clay or sand to a very high temperature, such as pottery, china, bricks and glass. Ceramics are hard and stiff, stay solid at very high temperatures and do not conduct electricity, but they are brittle.
Polymer

A substance made of very long chain molecules. Plastics are polymers, and most plastics are made from crude oil. Polymers are usually light, easy to mould into shape, waterproof and good insulators of electricity and heat; many are flexible, some are hard and stiff, and most soften or melt when heated.
Composite

A material made by combining two or more materials so that it has properties none of them has alone. It has a matrix (the material that holds it together) and a reinforcement (fibres or lumps) spread through it. Examples: fibreglass (glass fibres in a plastic), carbon fibre (carbon fibres in a plastic), concrete (stones and sand in cement), reinforced concrete (steel rods in concrete).
Hard
Hard to scratch or dent. A hard material is not always hard to break: a ceramic tile is hard but can shatter.
Brittle
Breaks or shatters suddenly, without bending first, when hit or bent. Ceramics such as glass and pottery are brittle.
Tough
Hard to break when hit or bent: a tough material bends or dents instead of shattering. The opposite of brittle.
Stiff and flexible
A stiff material is hard to bend; a flexible material bends easily. Ceramics are stiff; many polymers are flexible.
Insulator and conductor

An electrical insulator does not let electricity pass through it; a heat (thermal) insulator lets heat pass through only slowly. Polymers and ceramics are good insulators. Metals are good conductors of electricity and of heat.
Choosing a material
List what the job needs (for example light, stiff, waterproof, does not shatter, stays solid when hot), then pick the material whose properties match all of these needs, not just one of them.
Composition of the whole Earth
By mass, the Earth is made mostly of the elements iron, oxygen, silicon and magnesium. Iron is the most common element in the whole Earth, because the core is mainly iron (with some nickel).
Composition of the crust

The crust is made mostly of oxygen and silicon; by mass, oxygen is its most common element. Smaller amounts of aluminium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium make up most of the rest. Almost all of these are joined together in compounds: the oxygen in rocks and sand is not oxygen gas.
Ore

A rock that contains enough of a metal, or a metal compound, to be worth extracting. Most metals are found in the crust joined to other elements in compounds (often with oxygen); a few unreactive metals, such as gold, are found as the element.
Crust
The thin, solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth, about 5–70 km thick: thinner under the oceans and thicker under continents. It is the coolest layer.
Mantle

The layer below the crust, about 2900 km thick: the thickest layer. It is very hot rock that is mostly solid but can flow very slowly over millions of years. Magma forms only where small amounts of rock melt, near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
Outer core
The layer around the inner core, made of liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel.
Inner core
The centre of the Earth, made of solid metal, mainly iron and nickel. It is the hottest part of the Earth, but the enormous pressure there keeps it solid.
Tectonic plates
The crust and the top part of the mantle are broken into a number of huge pieces called tectonic plates. They move very slowly, a few centimetres a year.
Rock cycle
The slow processes by which rocks form, are broken down and are turned into other types of rock. Over millions of years any type of rock can become igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock.
Magma and lava
Magma is molten (melted) rock underground. Lava is molten rock that has reached the Earth's surface, for example from a volcano.
Igneous rock
Rock formed when magma or lava cools and becomes solid. It is made of crystals that fit tightly together (interlock). Examples: granite and basalt.
Crystal size and cooling rate

When molten rock cools slowly, for example magma deep underground, the crystals have time to grow large (granite). When it cools quickly, for example lava at the surface, the crystals are small (basalt).
Sedimentary rock

Rock made from sediment. Rock is weathered; the pieces are eroded and transported, then deposited in layers. The weight of new layers squashes (compacts) the sediment, and minerals in the water cement the grains together. It often shows layers and may contain fossils. Examples: sandstone, limestone and chalk.
Metamorphic rock
Rock formed when an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure, deep underground or near hot magma, without melting. Examples: limestone becomes marble; mudstone becomes slate.
Weathering

The breaking down of rock where it is. Physical weathering breaks rock up without making new substances, for example freeze–thaw: water in a crack expands as it freezes and widens the crack. Chemical weathering is caused by reactions, for example slightly acidic rainwater reacting with limestone. Biological weathering is caused by living things, for example plant roots growing into cracks.
Erosion, transport and deposition
Erosion is the wearing away and removal of pieces of rock by water, wind, ice or gravity. The pieces are transported, then deposited (dropped) when the water or wind slows down.
Fossil
The remains or traces of a living thing preserved in rock. Almost all fossils are found in sedimentary rock, because the remains were buried in sediment.
Finite (non-renewable) resource

A resource with a fixed amount on Earth that is not being replaced as fast as we use it, so it will one day run out. Metal ores, coal, oil and natural gas are finite: they formed over millions of years.
Renewable resource
A resource that can be replaced as fast as we use it, for example wood from forests that are replanted.
Recycling

Collecting, sorting and reprocessing used materials (for example melting scrap metal) to make new products. It saves raw materials such as ores and reduces waste, and it usually saves energy. Collecting, sorting, transporting and reprocessing also use energy, so whether recycling saves energy overall depends on these amounts.
Atmosphere
The layer of gases held around the Earth by gravity.
Composition of dry air

Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide, with tiny amounts of other gases. Real air also contains water vapour, which varies from almost none up to about 4%, so the percentages are given for dry air.
Air is a mixture
Air is a mixture of elements (nitrogen, N₂; oxygen, O₂; argon, Ar) and compounds (carbon dioxide, CO₂; water vapour, H₂O). Its gases are not chemically joined to each other.
Fossil fuels
Coal, oil and natural gas, formed over millions of years from the buried remains of living things. Burning them releases carbon dioxide.
Carbon cycle
Carbon moves between the air, living things, the oceans and the ground. Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air; respiration, decay and burning put it back.
Deforestation
Cutting down large areas of forest. Burning or rotting the wood releases carbon dioxide, and fewer trees remain to take carbon dioxide in by photosynthesis.
Greenhouse effect

Sunlight passes through the air and warms the Earth's surface. The warm surface gives off heat (infrared radiation). Greenhouse gases in the air absorb some of this heat and send some of it back towards the surface, so the Earth is warmer than it would be without them.
Greenhouse gas
A gas that absorbs heat given off by the Earth, such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour. Nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases.
Global warming and climate change

Extra carbon dioxide from human activity strengthens the greenhouse effect. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2021) states that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land: the years 2011–2020 were about 1.1 °C warmer than 1850–1900. Effects include rising sea level (about 20 cm since 1900), melting ice and more frequent heatwaves.
